To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the bile of a host species, when tested against the bile of a non-host species, is capable of causing the excystation of a non-host parasite, whereas the bile of a parasite-host species is incapable of doing so.

(a) bile salts are the major components of the bile of mammals and birds, (b) bile salts are essential for the survival of intestinal helminths, and (c) the bile salts of mammals, birds and reptiles are species-specific, and therefore the bile salts of one host species may be toxic to helminths of other species.
The host specificity of E. granulosus is determined by a single gene that encodes a protein, called the ‘major surface protein’ (MSP) of the parasite.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What properties are present in bile, and what are the functions of bile in the physiology of the alimentary tract of the host?
the following questions: (1) Do bile acids and other constituents of the bile play a part in the determination of host specificity in intestinal parasites?

the following aspects of bile: (1) the effect of bile on the development of the parasite in the host, (2) the effect of the parasite on the host's bile secretion and bile composition, and (3) the effect of parasites on host bile metabolism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these secretions are of little or no importance as factors in determining host specificity.

the chemical properties of the intestinal contents of the host are important factors in determining host specificity in intestinal parasites, but that the evidence for this is largely circumstantial and that the mechanisms are unknown.
the chemical properties of the bile are important in determining host specificity in intestinal parasites, and in the hatching and development of their eggs and larvae.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bile of the host is a major factor in determining host specificity in intestinal parasites.

the bile of a particular host is a factor in host specificity of the intestinal parasites of that host, but that the bile of one host is not necessarily a factor in host-specificity of parasites of another host.

the biochemical properties of bile, as determined by host species, play an important part, but not necessarily the only part, in determining the host specificity of the intestinal parasites studied, and that bile is an important factor in determining the specificity of hatching of helmins eggs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the host specificity of the parasite is determined by the host’s bile.
we have a new way to study the evolution of parasites.
bile acid metabolism and its regulation by FXR is an essential process in the maintenance of host health and that disruption of this pathway leads to the development of liver and gut diseases.
